conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey, doc. I’ve been having really bad pain on my right side again. It’s worse since I fell yesterday getting out of bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And this pain—does it go anywhere else? Like your chest or arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, sometimes it goes up to my right chest and arm, especially when I lift it. But the fall made it way worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see in your chart you had a seizure yesterday. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I think so. I couldn’t keep my meds down, and I’ve been having one every couple days lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve given you some Dilaudid for pain and Zofran for nausea. Your vitals are stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My wife usually helps me up, but she’s had surgery and can’t right now. That’s probably why I fell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll make sure you’re safe when moving around. We did a chest X-ray, and it looks clear—no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. But I’m worried about the pain. It’s not getting better like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. Your labs came back—white blood cell count is a bit high, but your lipase is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lipase? Isn’t that for pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but in your case, even during flares, it doesn’t always go up. Your history and symptoms point to another flare of chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not getting better even with the stents? I thought those would help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, the last ERCP showed the stent wasn’t helping and may have made the pain worse, so it was removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What now? I can’t keep living like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on pancreatic enzymes—Viokase—with meals to help with digestion. Also, a PPI to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using sustained-release morphine twice a day, with Dilaudid as needed for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. But what about my seizures? Neurology said something last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We got the video EEG results back—no epileptiform activity. Neurology thinks these are pseudoseizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pseudoseizures? So I’m not having real seizures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re real episodes, but not caused by abnormal brain electrical activity. Given that, we’re stopping all anti-seizure meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I was on Dilantin. My level was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your level was 1.6, which is low, but since the EEG shows no epilepsy, we don’t need to continue it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… that’s a lot. What about my diabetes? I take insulin at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your A1c is 6.6, which is good. But since your pancreas isn’t making insulin due to damage, we’re switching you to NPH insulin twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using 70/30. Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on half dose—10 units twice daily—to stay safe, especially since your appetite has been off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my stomach—still feels slow to empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing metoclopramide four times a day to help with gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I also have this nerve pain from an old electrocution injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting amitriptyline 25 mg at night for that neuropathic pain. It can also help with sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. Hope it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’ve been tolerating regular food well, and your pain is more controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I feel a bit better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. We’ll go over all your meds and follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my back pain? I have a nerve block appointment coming up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get info to schedule that here. We’re also adding stool softeners—Colace, Senna, and Miralax—to prevent constipation from the morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, I’ve been struggling with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re stable, pain is controlled, and you’re eating well. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I want to make sure I understand everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re stopping all seizure meds. Take the new insulin—10 units NPH twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the enzymes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Three capsules with each meal. Also, omeprazole three times a day with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about Clonidine? I take it twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now once daily for one week, then stop. Lisinopril will be your main blood pressure med.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain gets worse or I have another episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back to the ER. Especially if you can’t keep food down or have severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks, doc. I’ll follow up with GI and neurology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.
